title: 17 Tactics for Playing Workplace Politics and Moving Ideas
summary: Sean Johnson explains that workplace politics is not about manipulation, but about consensus building, execution, and navigating individual priorities. He shares 17 actionable strategies to pitch ideas, gain allies, and accelerate career advancement.
key_points: Reframe workplace politics: Politics is about execution, building consensus, and moving ideas through groups with different priorities.
Stop dropping raw ideas: Do not expect others to execute your idea sent over Slack or email when they have their own pressures.
Build a doer reputation: Make boring assignments impressive; people evaluate your ability to finish things as much as the idea itself.
Lead with story and pain: Frame proposals so the pain of staying put feels greater than the pain of change, as people decide emotionally and justify with data.
Use prototypes: Build docs, demos, or mockups using AI tools like Claude because tangible prototypes beat abstract ideas.
Sell laterally and down first: Gather grassroots support before pitching to leaders, and pitch your boss in private first.
Build broad support: Do not rely on a single champion who could leave; keep supporters updated and involved.
Co-create and convert critics: Let others help author solutions, never retaliate against criticism, and involve objectors in solving the problem to turn them into allies.
Start small for early wins: Focus on quick wins to build momentum, give credit away, and expand from there.

So, most people treat politics as though it is a dirty word. They think that it's something that like manipulative people or untalented people do to get promoted. And I thought that for a long time too. But I eventually learned that politics is really just about execution and building consensus and learning how to move ideas through groups of people who all have their own priorities. And I've worked with clients who were very, very good at this, at getting kind of the things done that they wanted to get done, and they move up in their organizations a lot more rapidly as a result. And so assuming that you want to be one of those people and be more effective, here are a bunch of ways to do it. First, stop being this guy. Like you have an idea, you open your email or Slack, you write a couple sentences, you drop the idea on everybody else and sort of expect them to take it and run with it. Those people, other people have other things they're working on and other pressures they're facing, and the last thing that they want to do is think about how to make your little fledgling idea happen. So don't be that person. What do you do instead? Number two, build a reputation as a doer. Take the boring assignment and learn how to make it impressive. People like to back ideas from people who they know will finish things. They're evaluating you as much as they are evaluating the idea itself. Number three, start with a story, usually about pain. So people like to decide emotionally and then justify with data. And so you want to make it clear that the pain of staying put is worse than the pain of whatever change you're proposing. Number four, know your stuff cold. Like anticipate all of their objections before they come up. Have data to back up your ideas. They might buy with emotions, but again, we justify with data. Number five, a prototype is worth a thousand meetings. So a doc, a demo, a mockup, anything tangible will beat something abstract, and that's much easier to do now with Claude and AI and all that. Number six, find someone who will call you out. Like you have blind spots, and you need a person who's going to be willing to tell you about them, ideally in private. Number seven, never retaliate.
